The chapter says this building is in Mumbai, and calls it the finest example of the Indo-Gothic architectural style that arose in India during the British period. It is also a World Heritage Site.

The other three pairs are correct: the Qutub Minar is at Mehrauli near Delhi, the Gol Gumbaz is at Bijapur (Vijapur) in Karnatak and the Taj Mahal is at Agra.

It is a natural human instinct to want to share one's experience, wisdom and emotions. When that instinct results in a beautiful creation, it is acknowledged as 'Art'. The artist's power of imagination, sensibility, state of emotion and skills are the crucial factors at the root of any artistic creation.

Artistic creations are of two types, Visual Arts and Performing Arts. The Sanskrit term for the first is Drik Kala and for the second Lalit or Aangik Kala. There are also two distinct traditions of art — Folk Art, whose expression is spontaneous and which is created by the collective participation of a social group, and Classical Art, which is expressed within an established frame of consistent rules and needs prolonged training to master.

The temples built in Maharashtra in the 12th-13th centuries are known as Hemadpanti temples.

Their plan is star-shaped: the outer walls have a zigzag design, which produces an interesting effect of alternating light and shadow. The important characteristic of a Hemadpanti temple is its masonry — the walls are built without using any mortar, by locking the stones together with the technique of tenon and mortise joints.

The Ambreshwar temple at Ambarnath near Mumbai, the Gondeshwar temple at Sinnar near Nashik and the Aundha Nagnath temple in the Hingoli district are a few of the finest examples of this style. Hemadpanti temples are found at several places in Maharashtra.

Maratha painting is an example of an art style. It began to develop in the latter half of the 17th century C.E.

The style consists of coloured paintings, and they occur both as murals and as miniatures used in manuscripts. Murals of the Maratha style can be seen in the old wadas at places like Wai, Menavali and Satara in Maharashtra.

The Maratha style was influenced by the Rajput and European styles of painting. Painting styles like this one help us to understand the life style, attires and customs of the times in which they developed.

The art market is an independent field. Buying and selling works of art calls for special expertise — someone has to assess the exact value of an art object and to ensure that it is genuine.

Neither of those judgements can be made without a deep understanding of art history, because the value and the genuineness of an object depend on knowing the period, the region and the style to which it belongs. That is why an expert with a deep understanding of art history is required in the art market.

Chitrakathi, also called the Pinguli tradition, is the tradition of narrating stories from the Ramayana or the Mahabharata with the help of wooden puppets and paintings. The pictures are drawn on paper and painted in colours made from natural substances, and it takes 30 to 50 pictures to complete the narration of a single story.

The tradition is very old — it is mentioned in 'Manasollas', or Abhilashitartha Chintamani, a book written by the Chalukya king Someshvara in the 12th century C.E. Along with Warli painting it is among the finest examples of the folk style of paintings in Maharashtra.

The pictures are preserved very carefully and handed down from one generation to another. Since the tradition is now on the verge of extinction, the artists and the government are trying to preserve it, so that this ancient art form and the history it carries are not lost.

The tradition of folk styles of painting closely resembles the style of rock paintings.

Rock paintings dating to the stone ages have been discovered in many countries. In India there are rock painting sites in Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Uttarakhand, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana; the rock paintings in the caves at Bhimbetka, a World Heritage site, are famous. They usually depict human, animal and geometric figures, and their style changed with the cultural change from the stone ages to the beginning of agriculture. Black, red and white colours made from natural substances were used. They tell us what ancient people knew about their natural surroundings and how they used the resources available to them.

Customs such as decorating house walls and courtyards (Rangawali) with figures and symbols, or using panels of paintings to narrate stories, helped regional styles of folk painting to develop.

The traditions of Warli painting and of Pingul or Chitrakathi in Maharashtra are among the finest examples of the folk style. Jivya Somya Mashe, an artist from Thane district, played a great role in making the Warli style popular; he received a number of national and international awards and was awarded the Padmashree in 2011. The Chitrakathi pictures are drawn on paper in colours made from natural substances, and 30 to 50 pictures are needed to narrate one story.

In the medieval period, under the patronage of the Muslim sultanates, many styles of architecture — Persian, Central Asian, Arabic and pre-Islamic native Indian — were blended together, and this blend created the Islamic architecture of India. Many beautiful buildings were created in it.

The Qutub Minar at Mehrauli near Delhi is one example. Its construction started during the reign of Kutubuddin Aibak in the 12th century C.E., four floors were completed in the reign of Altmash in the 13th century, and it was completed in the reign of Phiroz Tughluq. At 73 metres (240 ft.) it is the highest minaret in the world, and the Qutub Minar complex has been declared a World Heritage.

The Taj Mahal at Agra was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in the memory of his queen Mumtaj Mahal. It is looked upon as the paramount example of the beauty of Islamic architecture in India and has been declared World Heritage by UNESCO.

The Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur in Karnatak was built in the 17th century C.E. and houses the burial of Mohammed Adil Shah of Bijapur. Inside the dome after which the building is named there is a round gallery, where even a slight whisper can be heard everywhere and a clap echoes many times.

Art history is an independent branch of knowledge and various opportunities of research are available in it.

Art historians can work in the field of journalism. The art market is an independent field, which needs experts who can assess the exact value of an art object and confirm that it is genuine. Heritage Management and Cultural Tourism are recently developed fields in which students of art can find many professional opportunities; Museums and Archives Management, Library Science and Information Technology, Archaeological Research and Indology are important fields in this regard.

Applied art — an artistic creation given a utilitarian purpose — offers a further set of opportunities: industry and advertisement, interior design and the production of ornamental objects, art design of stage backdrops (Nepathya), art direction for films and television, layouts of books and magazines, calligraphy, and the production of greeting cards, invitation cards, customised stationery and gift objects. Architecture and photography are also part of applied art, as are computer-created still and animated graphics, ornaments, artistic creations in metal, decorated earthen pots, objects made from cane and bamboo, glass objects and attractive textiles and clothing.

Every one of these fields needs detailed planning and skilled, trained people at every stage of production, and the syllabi of art design courses therefore include the history of various industrial and cultural traditions. A few institutions in India offer technical and occupational training in these fields; among them the National Institute of Design in Ahmedabad, Gujarat is world renowned, and it has offered an online course since 2015.

The illustration is a Warli panel painted in white on a deep red-brown ground, of the kind the chapter describes as one of the finest examples of the folk style of painting in Maharashtra.

(a) Depiction of nature: trees fill the panel — a tall many-branched tree at the lower left, another spreading tree at the top centre, and smaller plants, leaves and saplings scattered throughout. Birds, fish and four-legged animals are drawn among them, so the natural surroundings of the people are shown everywhere rather than as a background.

(b) Drawings of human figures: the figures are built from very simple geometric shapes — two triangles joined at their tips for the body, a circle for the head, and single lines for the arms and legs. They are not portraits and carry no facial features; what they show is posture and movement.

(c) Depiction of occupations: the figures are shown in group activity rather than singly. They stand in long rows holding hands, some carry implements, some are drawn beside animals, and several are placed around the large decorated square at the centre of the panel, so the everyday collective life and work of the community is the subject of the painting.

(d) Houses: a few rectangular outlines appear among the figures, and the large square enclosure at the centre of the panel — drawn with hatched borders and a row of triangles along its edges — is the dominant built form in the picture. The houses are drawn in the same plain line style as everything else, with no attempt at perspective or detail.
